newsitem.title: CUBA: Hurricane Lili lashes Havana, downs power lines.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Lili lashes Havana, downs power lines.

text.p: Hurricane Lili lashed the Cuban mainland early on Friday as gusts of wind buffeted Havana, knocking down trees and power lines, eyewitnesses said.
Hurricane Lili pounded central Cuba with sustained 90 mph (145 kph) winds and torrential rains as the Bahamas braced for the coming storm, the National Hurricane Centre said.
At 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), the centre of Lili was located at latitude 22.7, longitude 81.6 west, about 35 miles (55 km) south-southwest of Varadero, Cuba, and moving northeast at about 8 mph (13 kph).
Lili crossed the Isle of Youth to the south of Cuba on Thursday night, with early reports indicating it damaged bananas crops but no casualties.
Strong gusts of wind were buffeting the Cuban capital and trees and power lines had fallen in parts of the city, eyewitnesses said.
At least 10 people were killed and hundreds driven from their homes as rain from Lili lashed Central America, rescue workers and local authorities said on Thursday.
So far the highest death toll was in Nicaragua, where Civil Defence officials said five people had drowned in swollen rivers across the country over the past four days and 200 were left homeless.
In Costa Rica four people were killed in river tragedies and in Honduras a young toddler died when his house was washed away in a shantytown on the edge of the capital Tegucigalpa.
A hurricane watch was in effect for the central Bahamas. A tropical storm warning remained in effect for the Florida Keys from Key Largo to the Dry Tortugas including Florida Bay.
Forecasters said Lili was expected to remain on its current track with an increase in forward speed during the next 24 hours, putting the eye over mainland Cuba on Friday and the Bahamas on Saturday.
In Cuba, the electricity company cut power to most parts of Havana before dawn to minimise damage to power lines during the passage of the hurricane.

President Fidel Castro, following the hurricane closely, travelled early on Friday to the southern coast in Havana province. The hurricane was expected to have a serious impact on the low-lying areas of the south coast of Havana and Matanzas provinces.

Thursday night Castro welcomed a group of people evacuated from their homes in Havana to make-shift dormitories set up in the Council of State, his office in Revolution Square. Earlier in the day, Castro had urged citizens to heed warnings to evacuate their homes if they felt the storm could destroy them.

Havana Communist Party first secretary Esteban Lazo said the rate of evacuations from vulnerable homes in a poor state of repair in Havana had improved and by Thursday night some 40,000 people had been evacuated. Earlier in the day many people appeared reluctant to leave their homes.
Havana international airport was closed late on Thursday until further notice and the national airline Cubana cancelled domestic and foreign flights for Friday.

But authorities were clearly worried by the reluctance of some Havana residents to heed advice to evacuate. Officials said that some 60,000 people should be evacuated from homes in a critical state of decay.
The hurricane is almost certain to be a severe blow to Cuba as it slowly emerges from the worst of economic crisis caused by the collapse of its old trade and aid partner the former Soviet Union.
Crops that may be affected include sugar cane fields. The cane, a crucial hard currency earner for Cuba, is within two or three months of being harvested.
